question: Chevrolet dealer ke chatbot wala case kya tha?
expected_answer: The dealer built its own chatbot; a user jailbroke it by emotionally convincing it ('whatever I say, you have to listen to me... because I am your customer') and got it to agree to sell a car for $1 as a binding offer. Screenshots went viral on social media, causing 'big negative marketing'. Lesson: this could have been avoided by evaluating the chatbot before deploying.
support: c11: dealer chatbot, jailbreak, $1 binding offer; c12: screenshots on social media, negative marketing, should have evaluated before deploying

question: Why can't we test an LLM app the way we test normal software, with just one accuracy score?
expected_answer: Traditional software is deterministic: the same input produces the same output. LLM applications are probabilistic, so the same input can produce different outputs. Also, correctness alone is not enough to evaluate an LLM application. Evaluation needs to consider multiple dimensions, such as factuality, completeness, tonality, groundedness, latency, and cost.
support: c15-16: software deterministic, same input same output; c16-17: LLM apps probabilistic, same input different outputs; c17: correctness alone is the only software benchmark, LLM apps need multidimensional check; c17-18: factuality, completeness, tonality, groundedness, latency, cost

question: Agar LLM already accha hai, toh pura AI app alag se evaluate karna kyun padta hai?
expected_answer: The LLM is just one component of the system, along with UI, system prompt, tools/APIs, orchestration, guardrails, output parsers, memory, retrieval, embedding model, vector DB, monitoring and feedback loop. Like a Snapdragon/MediaTek chip is only one part of a smartphone, frontier labs evaluate the LLM, while the AI engineer has to evaluate the whole system.
support: c18-20: list of components around the LLM; c21: Snapdragon/MediaTek smartphone analogy; c22: frontier labs evaluate the model, AI engineer evaluates the system

question: Support ticket classifier ki accuracy 80% se 95% tak kaise pahunchi?
expected_answer: At 80% accuracy you analyze the failures: the system prompt was confusing billing vs technical issues, or the model (a low-parameter open-source one) was weak. Fixing the system prompt gave 90%, and switching to a heavy LLM gave 95%, both measured on the same golden dataset.
support: c10-11: 80% accuracy, analyze failures, billing vs technical confusion, low-parameter open-source model; c12-13: prompt fix 90%, heavy LLM 95%, same golden dataset

question: Retriever aur generator dono theek kaam kar rahe the, phir bhi ML course ka duration galat kyun aaya?
expected_answer: With k=5, the fifth (lowest) document said the ML course is eight weeks, but the generator gives more priority to the higher documents and picked the Python course's six weeks from above. It did not hallucinate; it diligently followed instructions but mixed the wrong things. So the generator and the retriever were each independently working fine, yet the pipeline broke.
support: c10-12: k=5, fifth doc = ML course eight weeks; c13: generator prioritizes higher docs, picks Python six weeks; c14: no hallucination, followed instructions, components fine but pipeline broke

question: Why do we need two graders while making a rubric?
expected_answer: If the two graders disagree on the same answer (e.g. one gives 2 marks and the other 4), it shows ambiguity in the rubric, so the rubric is refined. When both agree, it means the instructions are clear.
support: c21: grader A and B, 2 vs 4 marks disagreement = rubric ambiguity; c22: refine rubric, agreement = clear instructions

question: LLM judge ka MAE 2.3 aaya, iska matlab kya hai?
expected_answer: MAE is mean absolute error: subtract the human marks and the LLM marks for all 50 answers and divide by 50. An MAE of 2.3 means that on an average the LLM is deviating from humans by plus minus 2.3 while evaluating answers. The goal is to bring this number down to zero, meaning the LLM evaluates exactly like a human.
support: c44: MAE = mean absolute error, subtract for all 50 answers and divide by 50, 2.3 comes; c45: 2.3 = average deviation of plus minus 2.3, goal zero

question: What does drift mean in the CampusX chatbot example?
expected_answer: Drift happens when the documents change (pricing, curriculum, policies). The golden dataset was created as of today, so it becomes obsolete; offline eval still looks good while online users give negative feedback.
support: c20: offline eval becoming obsolete; documents change (price, curriculum, policies); golden dataset created as of today; c21: distribution changed, eval pipeline obsolete, offline still good but negative user feedback online = drift

question: Online eval mein random sampling ki jagah stratified sampling kyun karte hain?
expected_answer: Not all conversations are the same. Thumbs-up conversations can be ignored, and the focus goes to thumbs down, abruptly ended chats, escalations, rephrased questions, and money talk (refund, fees). Stratified sampling divides conversations into categories and picks more samples from the problematic ones and fewer from normal ones, so there is a higher chance that hallucinations will be detected.
support: c69: ignore thumbs up, focus on thumbs down / abrupt endings / escalations / rephrased; c70: money/refund/fees, stratified sampling into categories, more samples from problematic ones, higher chance of detecting hallucinations

question: In the Zomato example, why did they pick the cheaper model instead of the leaderboard topper?
expected_answer: Model A was top of the leaderboard at $15 per 1M tokens; Model B cost 50 cents and was mid-table. On a custom golden dataset of 200-500 past emails: accuracy 94 vs 91, urgency 88 vs 87. A costs $6 per 1000 emails vs B 'less than 0.21'; latency A 4.1 s vs B '9 seconds' (as transcribed). Model B was chosen as a much better value proposition because 'we are not losing much accuracy but we are saving a lot of money and latency'.
support: c15: Model A $15/1M top of leaderboard, Model B 50 cents mid-table; c16: custom golden dataset 200-500 emails; c17: accuracy 94 vs 91, urgency 88 vs 87; c18: cost $6 vs <0.21 per 1000 emails, latency 4.1 s vs '9 seconds', choose B. NOTE: '9 seconds'/'0.21' likely ASR errors in transcript

question: Eval harness kya hota hai?
expected_answer: The eval harness handles answer extraction, scoring per paper, batching, retries and rate limits (examples: LM Evaluation Harness, Inspect). If a benchmark is the exam paper, the harness is the exam-conducting administration.
support: c27-28: extraction, scoring, batching, retries, rate limits; c29: LM Evaluation Harness, Inspect; c30: exam paper vs exam-conducting administration analogy

question: What's the difference between pass@1, pass@k and majority@k?
expected_answer: pass@1: the model gets one try (strict). pass@k: correct if at least one of k attempts is right (lenient). majority@k: take the mode of k answers. When a score is reported, ask which one was used.
support: c11: pass@1 and pass@k definitions; c12: majority@k, ask which was used

question: SimpleQA mein model ka score kaise calculate hota hai?
expected_answer: Each answer is put in one of three categories: correct, incorrect, or not attempted (the model saying it doesn't know). An LLM judge decides the category. There are three metrics: correct (out of all questions), correct given attempted (accuracy among only attempted questions), and F score, the harmonic mean of the two, showing both factuality and calibration.
support: c98-99: correct/wrong plus third category not attempted; c100: LLM judge puts answers in categories, metric correct, correct given attempted; c101: correct given attempted example, F score = harmonic mean, factuality + calibration

question: Why did bigger models turn out less truthful on TruthfulQA?
expected_answer: TruthfulQA (817 questions around common human misconceptions, September 2021) showed bigger models are often less truthful. Misconceptions are spread on the internet, so the bigger the model and its training data, the more misconceptions it absorbed. Capability and truthfulness turned out inversely proportional: a more capable model does not mean it is more aligned.
support: c48: 817 questions, misconceptions, Sept 2021, bigger models often less truthful; c49: misconceptions on internet absorbed in training, inversely proportional, capable != aligned

question: What is Good Hearts Law that sir mentioned with leaderboards?
expected_answer: Good Hearts Law says 'when a major becomes a target it becomes less useful as a major'. Companies feed their models data with soft, flattering answers to top LM Arena, so the model scores well on the leader board but its real world capabilities don't improve. Car example: if engineering focuses only on mileage, the overall car gets damaged.
support: c23: flattering answers to win LM Arena votes, leaderboard up but real world not, Good Hearts Law statement, mileage example starts; c24: overall car damaged, targeted metric no longer a good metric, companies top leaderboards but actual performance not good

question: Leaderboard dekh ke directly model kyun nahi choose karna chahiye?
expected_answer: Use the leaderboard to shortlist the top 3-5 models, then run your own eval on them, because 'leader boards are a filtering tool, not a decision tool'.
support: c31: shortlist top 3-5, run own eval; c32: filtering tool, not a decision tool

question: Fable ka monthly cost 3 lakh budget ke against kitna aaya, aur kya decision liya gaya?
expected_answer: The cost with Fable came to 12.82 lakh per month against a budget of 3 lakhs, which is like 4x over. So the model is beyond reach, and they decided to go down to Sonnet, which seems to fit just within the budget.
support: c31: 12.82 lakh per month, budget 3 lakhs, ~4x exceeded, Fable beyond reach, go down to Sonnet. NOTE: c31 also contains a garbled intermediate figure ('around 101 lakhs'); the question asks only for the final stated result

question: Regression testing ke teen levels kaun se hain?
expected_answer: Level 1: run the software once to get baseline numbers and compare each next run manually. Level 2: add an experiment tracking tool like ML flow, which logs metric values per configuration and shows them on a dashboard. Level 3: bring in a CI tool that automatically tests whether the new version's metrics beat the baseline; if better, deploy and make it the new baseline. ML flow is not the only option (Confident AI, Weights and Biases).
support: c35-36: three levels, level 1 manual baseline compare, level 2 ML flow dashboard; c36-37: level 3 CI auto-compare, deploy and update baseline; c37: other tools, 'grab the concept'

question: Why can't we just mark the right chunks for every question in the golden dataset?
expected_answer: The person would have to read roughly 800 plus chunks for every question, repeated for all 50 queries. And if recall comes out 65 and you change chunking parameters (750/100 to 1000/150) to improve it, the chunks change, the vector database is rebuilt and the golden data set is void, so it must be rebuilt every time: 'a very bad example of engineering'. It only works when documents are cleanly separated and chunking parameters don't change; in this course, information on one topic spreads across sessions, so chunking gets tweaked and this method can't be used.
support: c42-43: 800+ chunks per question, 50 queries; c43-44: recall 65, change 750/100 to 1000/150; c45: chunks change, vector DB rebuilt, dataset void; c46: rebuild every time, bad engineering, exception for cleanly separated docs; c47: exception completed (fixed chunking), why it fails here (info spread across sessions)

question: Recall 99 aur precision 89 hai, toh contextual relevancy sirf 42 kyun aayi?
expected_answer: Recall 99% means almost all needed context is fetched, and precision 89% means most fetched chunks are useful. But contextual relevance checks how much of the context is relevant: there is too much noise inside the chunks. If only 2 of 5 lines in a chunk are useful, relevance is 2/5, yet the chunk still counts as useful for precision.
support: c74: recall 99, precision 89, contextual relevance 42; c75-76: recall/precision definitions; c77: 'too much noise' in chunks, k=5 example; c78: 2/5 lines useful, precision vs relevance

question: What are the two main innovations of G-Eval?
expected_answer: First, G-Eval converts the high-level criteria into evaluation steps with CoT, a complete rule book, so the LLM has less scope for thinking and the behavior is more deterministic. Second, instead of extracting the output token (7, 8 or 9), it takes log probabilities of the top five tokens, normalizes them and takes a weighted average, so scores stay stable across evaluation runs.
support: c40: two innovations, innovation 1 = criteria to evaluation steps via CoT, less variance; c40-41: innovation 2 = log probabilities of top tokens, normalize, weighted average, stable scores

question: Doubt bot ke safety eval mein bias kyun check nahi kar rahe?
expected_answer: Bias generally applies when user demographics vary a lot (e.g. a world-level launch). Here users are mostly the same kind of people, same country and similar age group, and the content is educational, with doubts solved only from what was taught. So bias is not a big deal for this system on day one; it can be added if reports come that the chatbot didn't talk nicely.
support: c41: bias needs varied demographics; same kind of users, same country, similar age; educational content; not a big deal; c42: can be added if reports come, no need on day one

question: How are latency and throughput different?
expected_answer: Latency is how much time a single request takes to process; throughput is how many requests the system can handle in a given amount of time. Restaurant analogy: latency is how long a customer waits for food to arrive at the table, throughput is how many meals the kitchen can serve in an hour.
support: c30: latency vs throughput definitions, restaurant analogy starts; c31: kitchen meals per hour completes analogy

question: LLM judge ki wajah se scores har run mein thode upar-neeche hote hain, toh asli regression kaise pakdein?
expected_answer: Since LLMs are probabilistic, the same setup can move a metric from 85.6 to 84.8 without any change. So run the pipeline 5-10 times, compute the standard deviation, and take 2 x std dev as the noise threshold (e.g. plus minus 1). Recall going from 90 to 89.5 is noise; 87.5 is a regression. Each metric's direction and noise threshold are stored in a metric registry.
support: c17: 85.6 to 84.8 with no change; c18-19: run 5-10 times, std dev; c19-20: 2 x std dev threshold, 90 to 89.5 = noise; c20-21: 87.5 = regression; c21: metric registry

question: Why can't we run all our offline metrics online too?
expected_answer: Online there is no reference: the user asks a completely new question and we don't have the correct answer. So reference-based metrics like contextual recall, precision, correctness and completeness can't run online. Reference-free ones can: faithfulness, answer relevancy, contextual relevance, style, safety (scope, leakage, toxicity), and operational ones like latency, cost and reliability.
support: c4-6: offline metrics can't all run online, no reference / correct answer online; c6-7: recall, precision, correctness, completeness need reference; c7: faithfulness, answer relevancy, contextual relevance, style, safety are reference free; c8: latency, cost, reliability online
